initial_presentation: A 63-year-old male experienced a cervical spinal cord injury following a suicide attempt. No abnormalities were detected within the brain. Post-recovery, he was prescribed 20 mg/day of duloxetine by a psychiatrist for depression. The patient was referred to Takatsuki Hospital for ongoing treatment, where the duloxetine dosage was increased to 60 mg/day due to persistent symptoms of decreased motivation and depression, but no significant improvement was noted. The patient also experienced numbness in his hands and feet due to the spinal cord injury and was taking loxoprofen (180 mg/day) and pregabalin (225 mg/day) as prescribed by an orthopedic surgeon. Two years later, he reported continued numbness and pain in his extremities, along with dizziness and lightheadedness. A year after that, he had difficulty walking, fell down some stairs, and sustained a compression fracture of the lumbar vertebrae, leading to his admission to Takatsuki Hospital. Approximately four years after starting outpatient treatment at Takatsuki, his gait worsened, and cognitive function declined, prompting a transfer to the National Center of Neurology and Psychiatry for further evaluation. Neurological examination showed restricted upward eye movements, significant muscle stiffness in the right upper limb, and mild signs associated with the frontal lobe.

A 57-year-old male was admitted to an outside hospital with S-T elevation myocardial infarction (MI). During his stay, he experienced acute hypotension and required emergent central venous access through the right subclavian vein for vasopressors. He was stabilized at the outside facility. Two days later, he exhibited acute left hemiplegia and right gaze deviation. Transfer to our facility was arranged. During transport, he had a focal seizure and was intubated for airway protection. In the emergency department, his Glasgow coma scale score was 10 (E: 4, V: 1, M: 5). He was opening his eyes spontaneously. He had a right gaze deviation. He was localizing with the right lower and upper extremities but was plegic on the left side of his body. He experienced a cluster of seizures and was started on levetiracetam and propofol infusion.

A 17-year-old girl presented with a primary concern of retained deciduous teeth. Physical examination showed short stature, prominent frontal and parietal regions, a depressed nasal bridge, a beaked nose, underdeveloped midface, an obtuse mandibular gonial angle with relative prognathism, wrinkled skin over the fingertips, and nail abnormalities. Intraoral examination identified a deep midline antero-posterior ridge of the palate, a high arched palate, multiple retained deciduous teeth with caries, crowding, and enamel hypoplasia.

A 6-month-old female infant had presented five times to medical services since birth with a history of discharge from the umbilicus. On days 2 and 4, she presented with bleeding from the umbilical stump, which was managed with a pressure dressing.

The patient is a two-year-old girl born at full term to consanguineous Saudi parents via cesarean section due to breech presentation. She has a history of poor sucking, hypotonia, bilateral ptosis, and recurrent admissions to the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) for apnea. The family history is unremarkable. The clinical course began with a sudden cessation of breathing lasting more than 15 minutes, followed by a three-minute arrest. She also has a history of choking and coughing. Upon examination, the patient was afebrile, dehydrated, and pale, with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 3. Stabilization efforts were initiated, and she was intubated in the PICU.

A 48-year-old woman with uterine fibroids received her first subcutaneous injection of leuprorelin acetate, a GnRH agonist, at a dose of 1.88 mg on the third day of her menstrual cycle. Four weeks later, she received a second dose of the same medication. Six weeks after the initial injection, she experienced difficulty breathing and consulted her previous physician.

Patient 3 is a 69-year-old man with 17 years of education and a background as a retired middle school teacher. In 1999, while teaching a chemistry class, an individual entered the classroom, brandishing a firearm and making threats. The intruder forced the patient and students to listen to him for several hours until law enforcement intervened and apprehended the individual. Following this incident, the patient experienced significant distress, including anxiety, agitation, insomnia, and frequent crying.

A 33-year-old African American male presented with multiple nodular skin lesions, primarily located in the axilla and inguinal areas. He reported an increase in the number and size of draining pustules. The patient also experienced generalized joint pains, including swelling and redness in the left knee and right elbow. These symptoms typically occur 1 to 2 times yearly and subside with antibiotic treatment. On skin examination, generalized suppurate nodules and chronic scars were observed, along with sinus tracts in the intertriginous areas. Joint examination revealed effusions in the ankles, knees, elbows, wrists, and digits, with a notable swelling in the right second phalanx.

A 21-year-old female presented with asymptomatic dark skin lesions present since birth. According to her mother, the lesions initially appeared on the trunk and spread to the upper limbs, lower limbs, neck, face, and back within two years. The lesions darkened over time and stabilized after the age of 10, with no new lesions appearing. There was no history of erythema, vesiculobullous, or warty lesions before the onset of the pigmented lesions. The patient had no history of recurrent lower respiratory infections, cardiovascular issues, central nervous system involvement, developmental delays, or ocular abnormalities. Medical history included skeletal deformities since birth, right ear deafness since age 9, and primary amenorrhea. Chromosome analysis of peripheral blood lymphocytes performed in 2019 was normal. There was no family history of consanguinity, recurrent fetal deaths, or similar skin lesions. Systemic examination was normal except for musculoskeletal findings, which included scoliosis, short stature, syndactyly, brachydactyly of toes, sandal gap deformity of the left foot, and swan neck deformity of fingers. There were no dental anomalies, and secondary sexual characteristics were well developed. Dermatological examination showed multiple bilaterally symmetrical whorls of hyperpigmented macules along the lines of Blaschko on the chest, abdomen, and back, with similar linear lesions on the face, neck, and limbs.

A 27-year-old female with a history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, systemic lupus erythematosus, and end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis was admitted for acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Upper and lower endoscopies were planned.
